fixed.lead: Write an essay of at least 120 words in 30 minutes. In your essay, do the following.

example.purpose: 论述大学生参加志愿服务的意义与安排。
example.setting: Your college newspaper is collecting essays about volunteering. Some students worry that regular voluntary work takes time away from study. Write for fellow students about whether volunteering can be a useful part of college life.
bullets: State your view on volunteering during college.
Support your view with reasons and a specific example.
Suggest how students can balance volunteering with their studies.
must: 明确回答大学期间参加志愿服务是否有益，全文立场一致。
至少展开一条相关理由，并用具体情境说明志愿服务的作用。

lines.text: A small town library has opened a lending service for household tools after residents asked for help with occasional repair jobs. The collection includes basic equipment such as hammers and hand drills, but no electrical tools. Library staff said the decision followed a survey showing that many people bought tools they used only once. Adults with a library card can borrow up to two items for seven days without paying a fee. Before taking an item home, borrowers must attend a short safety demonstration at the desk. The tools were donated by a local repair group and checked by trained volunteers. Books will continue to occupy their usual shelves, while the new collection is stored in a separate room near the entrance. Staff will review borrowing records after three months before deciding whether to expand it. They stressed that the service provides equipment, not home visits or professional repairs for residents.

items.stem: What is the report mainly about?
options: A library replacing books with repair equipment.
A library starting a service for borrowing tools.
A repair group charging for visits to homes.
A town opening a shop for electrical tools.
items.why: 导语说明图书馆新增工具借用服务；原有图书仍保留，并非用工具替代图书。

items.stem: What must borrowers do before taking a tool home?
options: Donate an item to the collection.
Pay for a seven-day membership.
Visit a volunteer at home.
Attend a brief safety demonstration.
items.why: 原文要求借用前参加安全演示；七天是借期，不是收费会员期限。

lines.text: A riverside park has moved its weekly outdoor market to a nearby school yard while workers repair the main footbridge. An inspection found loose boards on the bridge, which normally provides the shortest route from the bus stop to the market. The bridge was closed before the market opened, and no injuries were reported. Organizers rejected a proposal to cancel the market because several farmers had already prepared fresh produce. Instead, the school offered its yard free of charge for two Saturdays. Signs at the bus stop now direct visitors along a different street, adding about five minutes to the walk. Delivery vehicles must arrive before eight in the morning so that the yard can remain free of traffic during trading hours. Repairs are expected to finish within ten days, but the market will return only after a final safety check. The park itself remains open through its other two entrances.

items.stem: Why was the footbridge closed?
options: Some of its boards were loose.
Farmers needed space to park vehicles.
A visitor had been injured there.
The school required a new entrance.
items.why: 检查发现桥板松动，因此封桥；报道明确说没有人员受伤。

items.stem: Why did organizers decide to keep the market running?
options: The park had lost both its other entrances.
Bus services had stopped for two Saturdays.
Farmers had already prepared fresh produce.
Repairs had already passed the final check.
items.why: 农户已备好新鲜农产品，是没有取消集市的直接原因；最终检查尚未完成。

items.stem: What must happen before the market returns to the park?
options: The school must begin charging a fee.
The bridge must pass a final safety check.
Delivery vehicles must stop using the yard.
The bus stop must move to a new street.
items.why: 回迁条件是通过最终安全检查；十天只是预计工期，不等于已经可以回迁。

lines.text: Hello, I'm organizing the photography club's exhibition. We booked the student hall for Friday, but the booking office says the floor needs repairs. Could the library help?
We have a meeting room upstairs. It holds thirty people, though we cannot allow pictures to be attached directly to its walls. What kind of display did you plan?
About twenty photographs, mostly local buildings. We expected visitors to walk around rather than sit through a talk. We could put the pictures on tables if necessary.
Tables would leave very little space for walking. We do have six standing display boards in storage. You could borrow them, provided someone collects them before Thursday afternoon.
That sounds promising. Is there a charge? We used nearly all our budget to print the photographs, so renting extra equipment would be difficult for us.
The room and boards are free for registered clubs. However, you must leave the room as you found it. Food is not allowed, although water is fine.
We can manage that. Our opening was advertised for six, and the library closes at eight. Would we have enough time to put everything away afterwards?
You can stay until half past eight to clear up. Please email the list of people helping you, so the evening staff know who should still be here.
I'll send that list this afternoon. First, I'll ask two club members to help collect the boards tomorrow morning. Then I can tell everyone about the new location.
Good. I'll reserve the room now. Once you have collected the boards, come to the desk and we will show you how to set them up safely.

items.stem: What are the speakers mainly discussing?
options: How to print photographs for a club.
How to find another venue for an exhibition.
How to repair the student hall floor.
How to attract members to a library club.
items.why: 原场地维修，双方讨论图书馆能否接办展览；照片已经印好，不是在商量印刷。

items.stem: Why does the library staff member suggest using display boards?
options: They can be attached directly to the walls.
They allow visitors to sit through a talk.
They are cheaper than printing photographs.
Tables would leave too little walking space.
items.why: 馆员指出桌子会占用行走空间，因而建议展板；墙上不能直接贴照片。

items.stem: What must the organizer send to the library?
options: The names of people helping with the exhibition.
A list of photographs that still need printing.
Payment for the room and display equipment.
A plan for serving food during the opening.
items.why: 馆员要求发来协助人员名单，便于晚间工作人员核对；场地和展板免费。

items.stem: What will the organizer probably do first after the conversation?
options: Move the exhibition back to the student hall.
Collect the boards alone on Friday evening.
Ask club members to help collect the boards.
Ask the booking office to delay the repairs.
items.why: 组织者说 First 要找两名社员帮忙次日上午取展板，之后再通知新地点。

lines.text: When a college gardening club took responsibility for a small vegetable plot, its members expected watering to be their simplest job. Instead, it became their first serious problem. Some plants received water twice in one morning, while others went dry for days. Everyone wanted to help, but nobody knew what the previous visitor had done. At first, the club leader proposed a strict daily timetable. Several members objected because their class schedules changed from week to week. Then a new member suggested placing a notebook in a waterproof box beside the gate. After each visit, gardeners wrote down the date, the beds they had watered, and anything unusual they had noticed. The system did not tell people when to come. It made their work visible to the next person. Within a few weeks, members were also recording broken tools and signs of insects. The notebook became a shared memory of the garden rather than simply a watering record. It did not solve every problem: somebody still had to buy seeds and arrange major repairs. Yet it reduced repeated work and helped new volunteers join in without waiting for instructions. The club learned that cooperation does not always require a more detailed schedule. Sometimes people need a simple way to see what has already happened and what still needs attention before they decide how to help.

items.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How a written record improved cooperation in a gardening club.
Why vegetable gardens need watering every morning.
How a club introduced a strict timetable for volunteers.
Why new volunteers should avoid major garden repairs.
items.why: 全文围绕记录本如何减少重复劳动、方便协作；严格时间表是被否定的方案。

items.stem: What caused the watering problem?
options: The club had no money to buy seeds.
The plants were all in the same bed.
Members did not know what others had done.
The notebook had been damaged by water.
items.why: 原文说没有人知道前一位来访者做了什么，因此出现重复浇水和漏浇。

items.stem: Why did some members object to a daily timetable?
options: They wanted to work only on major repairs.
Their class schedules changed from week to week.
They preferred to receive individual instructions.
They could not find a waterproof box.
items.why: 课程安排每周变化是反对固定时间表的原因；防水盒属于后来采用的方案。

items.stem: What can be inferred about the notebook?
options: It removed the need to buy gardening supplies.
It required volunteers to arrive at fixed times.
It replaced all decisions made by the club leader.
It helped volunteers choose useful work independently.
items.why: 新志愿者可不等指令就加入，说明记录帮助自主判断待办事项；它并未解决采购等所有问题。

groups.text:
Many students own tools that they use only once or twice a year. At one university, a student club decided to collect such tools and lend them out from a shelf in a dormitory hall. The idea was simple, but the shelf only began to (1) smoothly after a term of trial and error.

At first, the club accepted every donation. Soon the shelf was full of drills, hammers and sewing kits, but some of them were (2) and could not be used safely.

Keeping track of the tools was the next problem. In the first month, several items disappeared because nobody knew who had taken them. The club then introduced a simple online form, and every borrower now (3) the date and the name of the tool.

The form also showed which tools were in the greatest (4). Drills were borrowed almost every weekend, while the sewing kits were (5) taken off the shelf.

Some borrowers returned tools late or without their parts. Instead of charging fines, the club attached short (6) to each handle, explaining how to clean and pack the tool. Late returns fell (7) within a month.

The shelf has also changed how students think about their belongings. Several students have (8) that they used to buy tools they needed only once. Running the shelf costs very little, as the club spends only a (9) sum each term on batteries and spare parts. Still, for its members the real (10) of the project is not the money saved but the conversations that start at the shelf.

groups.label: Match each statement to a paragraph. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.
groups.text:
[A] A neighborhood association considering a shared workshop began with a simple question: what prevented residents from making small repairs at home? Its organizers expected to hear mostly about the price of tools. Instead, informal conversations revealed a mixture of difficulties. Some residents lacked a suitable table, others did not know where to obtain replacement parts, and several were afraid of damaging an object further. These answers changed the proposal. A room full of equipment would be useful only if people could also find guidance and a comfortable place to work.

[B] Before looking for a building, the association ran three Saturday sessions in a borrowed classroom. Residents brought small household objects and described what they hoped to do. Organizers noted the activities requested rather than counting every visitor as a future member. Someone who wanted help once a year would not necessarily pay a monthly fee. The sessions also tested a rule that owners should remain beside their objects during a repair. This made the work an opportunity to learn, while preventing volunteers from becoming an unpaid collection and delivery service.

[C] Finding a permanent room raised questions that were less exciting than choosing equipment. The association needed good lighting, reliable electricity, and enough space around each workbench. It also needed permission to use the room in the evening. A cheap basement was rejected because it could be reached only by a narrow staircase. A former shop was easier to enter but cost too much to heat. Eventually, a community center offered a room already used for daytime classes, on condition that all equipment could be locked away afterwards.

[D] Storage shaped the workshop's collection. Large machines would have occupied most of the available cupboards, leaving little room for materials used in common repairs. The organizers therefore bought a modest range of hand tools and kept a list of larger equipment available elsewhere. Each tool had a marked storage place, so a missing item was visible before the room closed. This arrangement also helped newcomers find what they needed without repeatedly interrupting an experienced volunteer. The aim was a manageable collection, not the largest collection the budget could possibly buy.

[E] Training began with tasks that appeared ordinary but could still be performed carelessly. Volunteers demonstrated how to hold an object securely, choose an appropriate tool, and stop when a job exceeded their experience. Nobody was expected to pretend to know every answer. When a resident brought in damaged electrical equipment, the group referred the case to a qualified repair service instead of attempting it. Turning work away was sometimes disappointing, but the organizers treated that decision as evidence of responsible judgment rather than a failure to offer help.

[F] The first publicity campaign showed finished objects beside their proud owners. Although attractive, the photographs gave some newcomers the impression that every visit would produce a successful repair. The association changed its notices to include objects that could not be restored and explanations of why. One example concerned a missing part that was no longer available. Another involved damage that would cost more to repair than the owner wished to spend. These accounts made expectations more realistic and allowed visitors to value an informed decision even when they left with an unchanged object.

[G] After two months, the attendance book showed that the early evening session was consistently quieter than the later one. Organizers initially considered closing it. A closer look at comments revealed that several regular users relied on those hours because they collected children later in the evening. Instead of judging the session only by its size, the group asked whether the timetable served different needs. It kept the early session but reduced the number of volunteers assigned to it. The change preserved access while avoiding unnecessary demands on the volunteer team.

[H] Money remained a practical concern. A small membership payment covered basic supplies, but visitors paid separately for any replacement parts they needed. The association explained this distinction when people booked a place, rather than waiting until a repair was under way. Donations were welcome, although donated tools were checked before entering the collection. The treasurer published a short account each quarter, listing income and the broad categories of spending. Residents did not need to understand accounting to see whether the project was meeting its ordinary costs or using up its reserves.

[I] The workshop gradually developed a record of recurring problems. Volunteers wrote brief notes about common faults, useful suppliers, and approaches that had failed. Names and contact details were kept out of these notes. A new volunteer could consult the record before attempting an unfamiliar task, and returning members did not have to explain every previous discussion again. However, the record was treated as a starting point rather than a guarantee. Objects that looked alike could differ internally, so each case still required inspection before any advice was applied.

[J] Not all benefits could be counted as repaired objects. A visitor might learn to maintain an item before it broke, find a local supplier, or decide not to buy equipment for a job that was beyond their ability. The association added a brief question at the end of each visit: what had become clearer? Answers were grouped by theme instead of being converted into a single score. This gave the organizers a fuller picture of the workshop's value without pretending that confidence, knowledge, and money saved were interchangeable results.

[K] The association's experience offered no universal formula for other neighborhoods. A community with many experienced volunteers might need different hours and equipment from one starting with very few. The most transferable lesson was the habit of making a limited proposal, observing its use, and revising it when evidence challenged an assumption. Sharing tools was only one part of the project. Sharing responsibility for how the service worked helped keep it useful. Growth was considered worthwhile only when the association could maintain the practical support on which existing users depended.

items.stem: A less popular time slot was retained because it met the needs of a particular group.
items.why: 人数较少的早场因接孩子的使用者需要而保留，只减少志愿者配置。

items.stem: The organizers distinguished occasional interest from willingness to pay regularly.
items.why: 试办时明确指出一年只需一次帮助的人未必愿交月费，并非将到场人数直接视为会员数。

items.stem: Users were asked what they had learned, even if the number of repaired objects did not show it.
items.why: 离场问题是哪些事情变清楚了，用于补充修好物品数量无法体现的收益。

items.stem: A limited amount of storage influenced the choice to buy mainly basic tools.
items.why: 储物空间不足使大型机器挤占常用物料位置，因此购买适量手工具。

items.stem: Initial discussions revealed that the cost of equipment was only one obstacle.
items.why: 最初访谈还发现工作台、配件来源和担心损坏等困难，设备价格不是唯一障碍。

items.stem: Written experience was useful, but similar-looking items still had to be examined individually.
items.why: 经验记录只是起点；外形相似的物品内部可能不同，每件仍须检查。

items.stem: Publicity was revised to show that leaving with an unrepaired object could still be a reasonable outcome.
items.why: 宣传加入无法修复的例子，并解释缺件或成本过高，使人理解未修好也可能是知情决定。

items.stem: People had to stay with their possessions while volunteers worked on them.
items.why: 试办规定物主留在物品旁，目的是学习，也避免变成代收代送维修服务。

items.stem: Expansion was acceptable only if support for current users could be maintained.
items.why: 末句限定扩张以维持现有使用者所需的实际支持为前提。

items.stem: Some jobs were passed to specialists instead of being attempted by workshop volunteers.
items.why: 损坏的电气设备转交合格维修服务，志愿者不做超出能力的工作。

careful.spec: All material must be original CET-4 level English for general university students: clear standard English, moderate sentence complexity, no specialist knowledge, living real people, current news, named real studies, unsupported statistics, copied passages, answer labels in explanations, or clues that reveal an answer before submission. Use consistent spelling within a passage. Fictional situations may illustrate a process but must not be presented as verified research. Every question has one provable answer. Chinese why must cite the decisive phrase or fact and explain the nearest competing interpretation. Use only the supplied point ids and cover all three in every set. Return only the requested schema fields, without id or model. Each item has an English stem, four distinct English options of parallel form, a zero-based answer, Chinese why, and point. Build distractors by changing the actor, time, cause, scope, condition, or purpose of a detail actually mentioned; each distractor must be refutable. Avoid absurd options, outside facts, all/none-of-the-above, double negatives, and answers identifiable by length. Distribute correct options across all four positions over the set; with five items use one position twice. Write one original 300–350-word explanatory or argumentative passage in 3–5 paragraphs. Topics: university learning, social behavior, work, technology, public services or the environment. Present a central claim, supporting explanation or a clearly hypothetical example, and a qualification. No title; count text only. Return one group, look passage, label exactly Read the passage and choose the best answer., full text, and exactly 5 items. Each set must include one main question about the whole passage, at least one explicit detail question, and at least one inference question. Vary the remaining questions among another detail, context-dependent word/phrase meaning, attitude, or rhetorical purpose; do not claim every set must contain all categories. Map factual retrieval and contextual wording to detail, whole-passage argument to main, limited inference/attitude/purpose to inference. Every item must be anchored to a distinct proposition or reading operation; no question should give another answer away. For vocabulary, quote a word or phrase that occurs verbatim and make every option fit the same syntactic slot. For purpose, explain how the example supports the surrounding argument, not merely what it says. For inference, do not add causality, certainty, frequency or scope absent from the text.

groups.label: Read the passage and choose the best answer.
groups.text:
Many people judge a public service by how quickly it completes a transaction. A short queue is certainly welcome. Yet speed alone may provide a misleading picture of whether a service is working well. A visitor can leave a counter in two minutes and still have no idea what to do next.

Consider a college office that helps students apply for financial support. In an imagined trial, staff replaced individual explanations with a printed checklist. Average appointment times fell, and the office initially regarded the change as a success. However, students whose family circumstances did not fit the standard examples began returning with the same unanswered questions. Each visit was shorter, but some students needed several visits to finish one application.

The difficulty was not that written guidance was useless. Most applicants found the checklist convenient, and staff no longer had to repeat basic information. The problem was treating the average length of a visit as a complete measure of quality. It counted each appointment separately, while students cared about completing the whole process. A system could therefore look efficient precisely because it passed unresolved work back to its users.

A better assessment would combine several kinds of evidence. The office could count how many applications were completed without a second visit, ask students whether the instructions were clear, and keep track of cases requiring individual advice. None of these measures would be perfect. A complicated case might take longer even when the service was excellent, and a satisfied visitor might still have misunderstood a rule.

The purpose of measurement should be to help staff investigate such differences, not to make every encounter identical. Fast service and thoughtful service need not be enemies. Written guidance can handle routine questions while staff spend more time on unusual situations. What matters is whether the arrangement helps people reach their actual goal, rather than merely moving them away from the counter.

items.stem: What is the author's main argument?
options: Short appointments always produce better public services.
Written instructions should replace personal advice.
Service quality should be judged by outcomes as well as speed.
Visitors should be responsible for solving unusual problems.
items.why: 首尾均指出速度不能完整反映服务效果，应看使用者是否完成实际目标；作者没有否定书面指引。

items.stem: Why did some students return to the office?
options: Their circumstances were not covered by the standard examples.
They wanted the office to shorten its checklist.
They had completed their applications too quickly.
They preferred to discuss rules unrelated to financial support.
items.why: 第二段说明家庭情况不符合标准示例的学生仍有问题未解决，因此再次来访。

items.stem: What does 'passed unresolved work back to its users' mean in the passage?
options: Asked students to help staff write new checklists.
Required staff to explain every rule several times.
Allowed visitors to choose their appointment times.
Left users to deal with difficulties the service had not resolved.
items.why: 前文的短预约未解决个别情况，学生需反复来访；此处指把未解决的问题留给使用者承担。

items.stem: What can be inferred about a long appointment?
options: It proves that written guidance is poorly designed.
It may be appropriate for a complicated case.
It shows that the visitor has understood every rule.
It should be divided into several shorter visits.
items.why: 第四段说复杂个案即使得到优质服务也可能耗时较长，所以不能只按时长判定低效。

items.stem: Why does the author discuss the imagined college trial?
options: To show why speed can give an incomplete picture of improvement.
To report a confirmed nationwide fall in service quality.
To prove that students dislike receiving written information.
To recommend using one identical procedure for every applicant.
items.why: 该例展示单次时长下降却仍需重复来访的矛盾；它是设想案例，并非全国调查结果。

translation.spec: 编写一道原创大学英语四级汉译英段落翻译题。setting 只放待译中文说明文，内容为中国历史、传统文化或社会发展，使用平实书面语和可靠的常识，避免未经核实的起源、年代、数字、疗效、名人和现实新闻。全文为一段，140–160 个汉字，标点不计，恰好 5–7 个完整句子，每句用句号结束；不含标题、拉丁字母、阿拉伯数字或提示译词，确保字符计数与汉字数一致。主题集中，句间逻辑清楚，包含可明确保留的主体、动作、时间或数量范围，以及转折、并列或因果关系；适合普通大学生译成自然英语，不需要专业术语。purpose 用一句中文概括主题。只输出 purpose、setting、must。lead 和三条英语指令固定，由系统加入：Translate every sentence. / Keep the meaning of the original. / Write natural, grammatical English. must 恰好三条中文，依次写明：本题每句话涉及的具体信息，不能漏译；本题必须保留的范围、时间、因果或转折，不能增译或译反；本题的英文主干与关键概念译法，允许自然的同义表达。三条对应教学反馈 meaning（完整准确表达信息）、structure（主谓明确的分句）、wording（按语境选词），不是官方分项权重。不要求学生补充理由或例子，不指定唯一译文，不写英文范文，不规定官方译文字数下限或上限，不加 id、model、to、subject、posts、bullets 或 lead。

fixed.lead: Translate the following paragraph into English in 30 minutes.
bullets: Keep the meaning of the original.

example.purpose: 介绍传统村落的生活与保护。
example.setting: 中国的许多传统村落依山而建，房屋与周围的自然环境相互协调。村中的小路不仅连接各家住户，也是人们日常交往的场所。过去，村民常在树下聊天，交流农事经验。如今，一些村落在保护老房子的同时，改善了供水和交通条件。游客可以了解当地的生活方式，但旅游活动也需要尊重居民的日常生活。保护传统村落，既要保存建筑，也要延续其中的文化。
must: 完整译出村落环境、小路的作用、过去的交流、设施改善、旅游与居民生活及保护的两方面。
保留“许多”“一些”“过去”“如今”和“既要……也要”的范围与关系，不擅加年份或数量。
合理组织英文分句，准确表达 traditional villages、water supply、local culture 等概念，允许同义译法。
